title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad
description: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "desp
body: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable". Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done". In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.The ad set off a storm of criticism from members of both parties. On Thursday, President Donald Trump sought to defend it and Ramaswamy on social media.Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.  "I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening. "You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad. The last time Acton saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted, according to Acton's campaign.Arthur's husband fled the state before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004. Arthur left with him.In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".Trump, who has endorsed Ramaswamy,  blamed the press for the negative reaction to the ad, in a long post where he also commended Arthur and Ramaswamy. Trump blasted DeWine, as well.He urged Ramaswamy to keep up his attacks and "let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!""I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse," Trump also posted.In the ad, Arthur repeatedly says Acton lies and asserts she "needs help", but does not discuss anything related to cheating or stealing.Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor."And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense".He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour.A poll by VoteHub, external released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad.If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades.

schema.headline: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad

title: Brazilian election: Lula seeks Bolsonaro's disqualification over alleged Meta interference
description: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up t
body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts". "Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read. Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally. Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted. Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network". The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power". He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes. Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

schema.headline: Brazilian election: Lula seeks Bolsonaro's disqualification over alleged Meta interference

title: Durban attack: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
description: A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.According to police, the unidentified ma
body: A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established.The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg.Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year.One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries.These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence.Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month.Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals. His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated.One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic."We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.Additional reporting by Pumza Fihlani in Johannesburg

schema.headline: Durban attack: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa

title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
description: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, feari
body: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid."With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS Now, external. In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation. The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS Now, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out." Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed."We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one. She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating. Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it"."You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

schema.headline: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out

title: Irish government minister criticises rape crisis centre consent ad
description: It's the consent campaign that's sparked heated debate across Ireland and beyond  - so why has a social media ad about getting a hug from your grandpa
body: It's the consent campaign that's sparked heated debate across Ireland and beyond  - so why has a social media ad about getting a hug from your grandparents been pulled?The ad, described by an Irish government minister as "demeaning to grandparents", sees a house's front door opening to reveal an elderly couple.They hug their grandson and lean into embrace their granddaughter, who looks uncomfortable before it quickly cuts to a graphic and voiceover. "Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely."The tone is light-hearted, and the aim is to promote the importance of consent for children - but it has apparently landed with a thud in Ireland and with many online.The ad, one of three, is part of a campaign called We-Consent, run by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC).The backlash has opened up a debate about changing norms, the role of family and how best to teach consent to children. While some have described it as a waste of money, others have defended it as showing how children have differences when it comes to boundaries and that it is "not campaigning against grandparents".Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan has been an instrumental critic - his department is one of the sources of funding for the campaign and its removal came after his officials intervened. He said the video "does not represent the views of the government"."It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them."While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."In a statement to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, the DRCC said the videos were "premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too"."We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have," it added.Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill, who is among the critics, said the video was a waste of resources."What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," he said, adding that this "publicly-funded social media video is a million miles off the mark". "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said the videos were "produced by DRCC at low cost using volunteers and are not part of a government advertising campaign".Meanwhile, Dr Eoin O'Malley, an associate professor at Dublin City University, said he believes the advert is the latest example of the state overreaching. "You are seeing people pushing ideas that are beyond mainstream," he said.O'Malley said that the importance of consent is reasonable to most people, but that the video is too extreme."The idea that there needs to be an ad telling grandparents that they shouldn't hug their grandkids, that they should look for permission in advance of that, seems absurd to most normal people."The Irish constitution is very clear that the family is the primary unit for teaching children and for raising children, and so to some extent this is kind of going beyond that."However, the campaign has its defenders too.Academic Dr Órfhlaith Campbell said it is not an attack on grandparents but instead aimed to highlight the importance of consent."The ad is highlighting differences in children's needs and the imp (sic) of consent. It is not campaigning against grandparents. Dear god in heaven!!!" she wrote on X, external. An account named Danny Boy said it wasn't "discouraging grandparents from hugging children" but was "encouraging children to speak up" if they feel uncomfortable.

schema.headline: Irish government minister criticises rape crisis centre consent ad

title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
description: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on
body: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data."The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people. "Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.  To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock. Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

schema.headline: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy

title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
description: Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime mini
body: Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory. There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.

schema.headline: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?

title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
description: Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.Th
body: Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe. Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board. It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.   Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.  With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.  Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.  It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

schema.headline: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax

title: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots
description: Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this
body: Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected.France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said. Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la République, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday.Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses. The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT). Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday."The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests. Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

schema.headline: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots

title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
description: Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.Trump ma
body: Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks.Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back."The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.Ukraine relies on Starlink - owned by Musk's SpaceX company - for a range of battle communications and early warning systems during Russian missile attacks.Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink. The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials. The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation. BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.  Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October. Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

schema.headline: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network

title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
description: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a p
body: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.But that may end soon.Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally."Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business. A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level."A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders. Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants". While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible. While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP). Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies."This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work."Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

schema.headline: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream

title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
description: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming langua
body: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out."The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue"."But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented"."It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date."Hacking has been around for many years," he said."The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long."MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today. PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced."That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally."The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group."A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue."Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other"."Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

schema.headline: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found

title: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?
description: Figure caption, How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?ByLiv McMahonTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdate
body: Figure caption, How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?ByLiv McMahonTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 12:15 BSTFor more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".What is PHP?Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server.Developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, PHP still powers lots of platforms today, including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites.When you visit a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation, external, composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity".What is the vulnerability?A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet.Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected.Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found".Wiz wrote in a blog post, external about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed.AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites.What websites have been affected?The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.Image source, EPAImage caption, Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on WednesdayA number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.What happened after the flaws were exposed?The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years."All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database."These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X. "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.Tech companies have also sought to quickly secure their systems.E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue, but its websites were operating as normal.Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, also said it had seen "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced."That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, external.How was AI involved?Researchers at Calif and Wiz who located the vulnerabilities used advanced AI tools which can analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said."The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure."Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.What does it mean for you?The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users - meaning most people won't need to take any action.But small businesses with sites, including those built using WordPress, may be wondering how to protect themselves.Those who own websites or manage infrastructure running PHP have been urged to secure their websites by updating to the latest version.Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes - known as patching - is "a bit like running a Windows update".If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied - something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins.If you look after your website yourself, Munro says "it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied".The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends, external considering temporarily taking sites offline if updates or temporary protections cannot be applied quickly enough.The US National Security Agency has also urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks, telling people to closely monitor updates from software vendors."Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said, external.And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

schema.headline: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?

title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
description: Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East corre
body: Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromNazarethAt rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties."I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."Image caption, All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab partiesMost opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.Image caption, Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity.  Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.Image caption, Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab partiesAt Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party. I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties."In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings. These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.Image caption, United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence"While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc. For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government."We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me. "That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Joint List talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace Netanyahu's governmentMeanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition. It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime. In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for. Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.Image caption, Arab Israelis accuse the government of inaction on the issue of gang crimeIn Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November. No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction."It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness.""As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."Image source, Ziad SamouniImage caption, Ziad Samouni's son Hussein (2nd L) was shot dead last November but no arrests have been made This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

schema.headline: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks
description: Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, bu
body: Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.  Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.

schema.headline: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks
